articles.title: A walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’
articles.summary: The famous pueblos blancos in southern Spain’s Sierra de Grazalema natural park teem with wildlife amid a limestone wonderland of peaks. ‘The wind is in from Africa / Last night I couldn’t sleep.” Joni Mitchell has ear-wormed her way into my head as my wife and I step out from Zahara de la Sierra…
body: Either way, Africa feels present as we tramp through the countryside of Andalucía, if only in the wildlife. The painted lady butterflies drifting over the flower-spangled verges, the turtle doves purring from the olive groves and the booted eagle drifting overhead: all are summer visitors recently blown in from the great continent to our south.

It’s day two of our White Villages of the Ronda Mountains walking tour, a self-guided seven-day route from On Foot Holidays that explores this alluring corner of southern Spain. We arrived yesterday by bus from Málaga, winding up through the mountains until the whitewashed dwellings of Zahara appeared like teeth in the hillside ahead. This was the first of the week’s four pueblos blancos, all tucked picturesquely into the natural park’s rugged 51,695 hectares (127,740 acres) of limestone peaks and serpentine river valleys.

I’ve walked with On Foot before, so the routine is familiar: water bottles and packed lunches stashed in daypacks, laminated map around neck on lanyard and route app open on phone (belt-and-braces navigation). Best of all, our luggage is already wending its way by taxi to the next destination.

articles.title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreads
articles.summary: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads. Few things make me happier than a bowl of warm musabaha served with freshly baked bread straight from the pan.
body: When I’m short of time but craving something nourishing, full of flavour and genuinely satisfying, I turn to murabaha time and again. Unlike hummus, the chickpeas are left whole, then gently warmed and topped with a vibrant salad of spicy cherry tomatoes, fresh coriander and good olive oil. Serve with plenty of the warm flatbreads below for scooping.

Put the chickpeas in a medium saucepan with enough water just to cover them., put on a medium heat and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook for about five minutes, just to soften them a bit more, then drain, reserving about 300ml of the cooking liquid.
Meanwhile, put all ingredients for the cherry tomato salad in a medium bowl with half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.

Put the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring often, for two minutes, until the garlic starts to colour, then add the chilli and cook for another minute. Add the drained chickpeas, the reserved cooking liquid, cumin, tahini, yoghurt, lemon juice and a teaspoon of salt, bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer, stirring from time to time, for two minutes.
points: This rubbly cousin of hummus is flavourful and satisfying at any time of day, served warm, topped with a colourful salad and just made to eat with homemade flatbreads.
Few things make me happier than a bowl of warm musabaha served with freshly baked bread straight from the pan.

articles.title: Caregiver creep: how helping elderly relatives can snowball into a full-time job
articles.summary: Assisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more support. Helping an ageing parent or loved one often begins with easy-to-field requests: Pick up a prescription. Drive them to a doctor’s appointment. Grab groceries.
body: However, light tasks – just “helping out” here and there – may eventually snowball into the avalanche of full-time caregiving, a phenomenon becoming known as “caregiver creep”. Like “ caregiver burnout ”, it’s not a formal term, but there is growing awareness about this slow build among healthcare providers and experts.

A 2025 research report from the AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans act as caregivers; one in every four adults is a caregiver and the majority (94%) are caring for an adult. As the population ages – the oldest baby boomers will turn 80 this year – the need for care will increase.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports the majority (59%) of those providing this unpaid care are women. Many gen X and millennial women are feeling the sandwich-generation squeeze of caring for parents and children on top of their careers.

Recognizing when responsibilities increase, how to identify when support needs to level up, and where to find resources both for the person receiving care and the caregiver can help manage caregiver creep.

articles.title: A job that changed me: Being a theatre usher cracked open my heart to beauty
articles.summary: The performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviour. I was 24, had just moved into a share house I couldn’t afford, and my job as a nanny was proving less than ideal.
body: A friend had told me to apply to become a front-of-house staff member at Australia’s busiest performing arts centre, Arts Centre Melbourne. It was a rare opportunity, as people rarely quit. To be surrounded by art again sounded like a dream.

I progressed to the final interview round. Anxious about nailing it and unable to study for it – for some unknown reason, a maths quiz was involved – I focused purely on appearance. I blew my budget on a blow wave, planning to charm the interviewers with my perfect hair and Target office-casual best.
Whether it was my hair or the secret texts to my friend asking for help answering the maths quiz, I got the job.

articles.title: From the Archives: Brad Johns, the Color Czar
articles.summary: Brad Johns, the celebrity colorist known for his “chunking” technique and influential work with Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, died last week at his home in Los Angeles. Revisit Vogue’s profile of Johns from the July 1995 issue, titled “The Color Czar.”
body: Here, revisit Vogue’ s July 1995 profile of Johns, titled “The Color Czar,” by Vanessa Friedman.

“My mission on this planet is to make people’s hair look good,” Johns says, running a hand through his own yellow-brown, blow-dried, shoulder-length locks. “Everyone’s hair, no matter what the exact tint, should be bright, beautiful, and expensive-looking.”

As it happens, this is a good time to be someone who wants to make everyone’s tresses bright and beautiful. Faux hair color, from platinum to black, has never been so big: Model Shalom stole the spring shows when she went from her natural plain brown to ebony; three of People ’s Most Beautiful People are bright fire-engine redheads; and even O.J. prosecutor Marcia Clark has used color to give her case an added boost. When glamour replaced natural as the look of choice, hair—and its power to call attention, decorate, and define—gained new potency. And that gave top colorists al-most incalculable authority.

articles.title: The First AllSaints Collection by Aaron Esh Drops Today
articles.summary: Aaron Esh descirbes his new AllSaints collection as “a real wardrobe worn by real people, inspired by the kids who are out there with music that’s loud.”
body: That’s spot-on for the AllSaints, of course. Since it opened its first store in 1997, AllSaints proliferated as a go-to fixture for kids on the hunt for ready beaten-up biker jackets, scraggly t-shirts, and skinny dirty-wash jeans, a brand that became a wish-fulfillment club for aspiring indie rockers everywhere. That’s the other point that commentators have got excited over: how Esh’s job fits into a bigger pattern upending the luxury fashion order: the surge of designer appointments to high street brands with an international reach, which includes Clare Waight Keller at Uniqlo, Zac Posen at Gap, and John Galliano at Zara.

articles.title: Can Aaron Esh Make AllSaints Cool Again?
articles.summary: CEO Peter Wood met Aaron Esh in a chance encounter at the Fashion Awards in 2024. Now, he’s giving the designer full creative freedom to reset the label.
body: It’s midday on a Wednesday at AllSaints HQ, a former industrial warehouse in London’s East End that, for some three decades, has housed the British premium brand. Designer Aaron Esh, a city native known for his buzzy namesake label, is finalizing almost a year’s worth of work as AllSaints chief creative officer, ahead of the big reveal on September 1. The question is, can Esh make AllSaints cool again?

Across the globe, current brand sentiment toward AllSaints varies, a company representative shared. In Asia, the positioning is stronger, and the brand is considered high end. But for many Brits, AllSaints had its heyday during the 2000s and early 2010s, when it was associated with the typical tropes of indie sleaze style — “Jesus Loves” studded belts, military boots, and distressed jeans — as well as the popular youth culture TV series of that era, Skins. Across the rest of the world, it holds a stronger image.
A big part of Esh’s vision lies in elevating the brand in both quality and look.

articles.title: In Guadalajara, Chasing Art, Fantastic Food, and the Love of a Good Time
articles.summary: Mexico's second city is the birthplace of many of its cultural cornerstones, from mariachi to tequila. Longtime visitor Michael Snyder returns to dive deep into its world-class culinary and craft scenes.
body: The second day of my first trip to Guadalajara, a decade ago, began, like so many mornings in Mexico's second city do: with blazing sunshine and a blazing hangover. I'd spent the previous evening sipping agave distillates at Mezonte, a miniature plywood-clad tasting room that pours some of Mexico's most exciting spirits, and dancing clumsily at what may be the world's most perfectly named bar: Pare de Sufrir, or Stop Suffering. My inevitable headache required an antidote. And so, in the fine expiatory fashion of this famously Catholic, famously hedonistic metropolis of nearly six million, I chose sublimity.
The ornate Guadalajara Cathedral mixes neo-Gothic, Baroque, and Spanish Renaissance architectural styles.
Murals by José Clemente Orozco adorn the central dome of the Hospicio Cabañas.

articles.title: The Marketer’s Guide to Choosing the Right Influencer
articles.summary: Where once reach and following were the be-all and end-all, creator marketing metrics have shifted. Today, brands that want to capitalize on influencers need to choose differently, leaning into the micro economy.
body: This article is part of the Business of Influence series, examining the inner workings of content creation and how the industry is set to change in the years to come.

Influencer marketing is changing — leaning toward snacky, messier, more niche formats and away from massive followings as the be-all and end-all. As social media trends move faster than ever, picking the right creator to partner with on a campaign has become a complex web of considerations for brands, with a cottage industry of agencies designed to help them do so, down to the micro and nano level, at scale.

Sometimes, no amount of marketing research can predict where the algorithm will go next. Chanty Beluga, the fictional character made up by online comedian Courtney O’Donnell, debuted on social media on July 28 in a skit titled “Actress named ‘Chanty Beluga’ doing a self-tape”. The bit went viral over a series of similarly formatted clips, and less than a month later, O’Donnell has landed a partnership with Verizon.
points: Where once reach and following were the be-all and end-all, creator marketing metrics have shifted.
